dimension: Volunteer and distributed computing work allocation — BOINC, SETI@home, Folding@home, Einstein@Home, HTCondor ClassAds, grid and desktop-grid scheduling, and peer-to-peer reciprocity
summary:
This field has been solving exactly the founder's problem since 1999, and it has published both the mechanisms and the failures. The canonical answer to "allocate work across wildly unequal, untrusted participants" is BOINC's score-based matchmaking: a weighted linear sum S(J,H) of named terms, computed per (job, host) pair, with projects free to reweight or replace the function entirely (Anderson and Reed, "Celebrating Diversity in Volunteer Computing", HICSS-42, 2009, section 4.8). Capability is never a vendor name; it is `proj_flops(H,V)`, the sample mean of runtime divided by an a-priori job-size estimate, maintained per (host, app version) pair, with a documented fallback ladder when samples are short: use the per-host mean if samples exceed a threshold (currently 10), else the per-app-version mean across all hosts, else a static peak-FLOPS prior (Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 6.3). That ladder IS a cold-start solution, and it is hierarchical shrinkage, not a tournament.

Heterogeneity is handled by job-size matching, not by ranking: BOINC computes each host's effective speed, sorts the population, finds quantile points, and sends size-class i jobs to hosts in the ith quantile, with the scoring function penalising mismatch by -(A-B)^2 in standard-deviation units (HICSS-42 section 4.5; BOINC JobSizeMatching wiki). This is the literal answer to "it doesn't make sense to pitch a little desktop PC against a vast supercomputer".

Trust cold start is adaptive replication: a pessimistic prior plus mandatory probation. As formalised by Christoforou et al. (arXiv:1307.2783, Figure 1), the older BOINC scheme sets error rate beta(0) = 0.1, multiplies by 0.95 on each valid result, adds 0.1 on each error, and grants trust only below 0.05; the current scheme gives reputation 0 until a streak of 10 consecutive validated results, then 1 - 1/streak.

Two mechanisms in this literature are nearly identical to what the founder proposed, under different names: BOINC "probe jobs", executed exactly once on every host with the output stored in the host record and read by the project's scoring function (HICSS-42 section 4.9), and Sarmenta's spot-checking, which injects tasks with known answers into the ordinary workload (FGCS 18(4):561-572).

mechanisms.name: BOINC probe jobs ("assigned jobs")
mechanisms.what_it_does: A project supplies a job that "is executed exactly once on all hosts". Its output, typically an XML document, is stored in the host record in the database and can be referenced in a project-specific scoring function. It exists precisely for scheduling decisions BOINC itself cannot make from reported hardware attributes.
mechanisms.citation: Anderson, D.P. and Reed, K., "Celebrating Diversity in Volunteer Computing", 42nd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS), section 4.9 (PDF at boinc.berkeley.edu/boinc_papers/hicss_08/hicss_08.pdf; Anderson's own 2019 reference list dates it HICSS '09)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Fully: the probe runs on every participant on first contact, before any ordinary work is routed, and its result is persisted in the participant record. This is the founder's calibration task, already named, already implemented, already wired to a scoring function.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The probe output is arbitrary project-defined data consumed by a project-defined scoring term, so any capability dimension can be probed, not only speed.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers almost without change: a hard randomly-generated mathematics problem run once per seat, with the graded result written to the seat record and read by the routing score, is this mechanism. Two things break. First, BOINC runs the probe ONCE and never again, so the resulting figure is a static snapshot — the founder's constraint that capability is measured, not assumed, is then only satisfied at t=0. Second, and more importantly, BOINC's mainline capability estimate deliberately does NOT use probe output; it uses observed runtimes on real jobs (proj_flops). The designers had the probe mechanism available and still routed by live work statistics, because a probe measures performance on the probe.

mechanisms.name: proj_flops(H,V): per-(host, app version) measured capability with a documented cold-start fallback ladder
mechanisms.what_it_does: The server maintains, for each host H and app version V, the sample mean and variance of (runtime(J) / est_flop_count(J)) over all jobs J processed by H with V, and also the per-app-version mean across all hosts. Capability is resolved in three tiers: if the number of (H,V) samples exceeds a threshold ("currently 10"), use the per-host mean; otherwise if the per-version mean has enough samples, use that; otherwise use peak FLOPS, the sum over processing resources of usage times that resource's peak FLOPS.
mechanisms.citation: Anderson, D.P., "BOINC: A Platform for Volunteer Computing", arXiv:1903.01699, section 6.3; also BOINC wiki "RuntimeEstimation" (github.com/BOINC/boinc/wiki/RuntimeEstimation), which gives estimated_flops = 1 / host_app_version.et.avg and notes the per-project duration correction factor (DCF) is "no longer used"
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By hierarchical shrinkage, not by a tournament. A brand-new participant inherits the population mean for that task type; if even that is thin, it falls back to a cheap static prior (declared peak capability). No ranking round is run, and no capacity is spent on calibration.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Capability is a vector indexed by (participant, task type), never a scalar per participant. Anderson's stated reason for the (host, app version) granularity is that "some computers are reliable for CPU jobs but unreliable for GPU jobs".
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and is the strongest competitor to the founder's cold start. It says: do not hold a calibration round at all. Route the first jobs using a cheap declared prior, record runtime-per-unit-of-declared-difficulty for every real job, and switch to the per-seat estimate once 10 samples exist. What breaks if adopted: the founder loses the up-front ranking, and the first roughly 10 jobs per (seat, task type) are routed on a prior that may be wrong. The mitigation in the literature is replication over those jobs, not a tournament.

mechanisms.name: Job size matching / multi-size apps (size classes and quantiles)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Projects create jobs in a range of sizes. A size_census daemon computes each host's "effective speed" as hav.et.avg * host.available_frac, sorts the population, and finds quantile points, which the feeder loads into shared memory. The scheduler then "will try to send jobs of size class i to devices whose effective speed is in the ith quantile", and "failing that, it should preferentially send jobs of smaller size classes rather than larger". In the earlier formulation, a host whose throughput differs by X standard deviations from the mean is sent jobs differing by approximately X standard deviations from the job-size mean, with the scoring term -(A-B)^2 where A is job size and B is host speed in standard-deviation units. A size_regulator daemon holds jobs INACTIVE and releases them per size class between low- and high-water marks.
mechanisms.citation: Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.5; BOINC wiki "JobSizeMatching"; Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 3.5 — "The difference in performance between volunteer devices ... can be several orders of magnitude. A job that completes in five minutes on one could take a week on the other." Throughput in World Community Grid was measured as varying by 2 orders of magnitude.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Poorly, and the gap is undocumented. The JobSizeMatching page gives no fallback for a host with no history; effective speed cannot be computed from hav.et.avg without samples. In practice the host falls through to proj_flops tier 2 or 3.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This IS the heterogeneity mechanism, and it is the exact answer to the founder's desktop-versus-supercomputer constraint. Rather than excluding weak participants, it gives them proportionally smaller work so that every participant's wall-clock turnaround is comparable (the stated target is job runtime "on the order of an hour").
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and is more useful to CDSFL than ranking is. It reframes the goal: do not decide WHO is best, decide WHICH SIZE of claim each seat gets, so that all seats return in comparable time. What breaks: it requires the task generator to produce a controllable distribution of claim difficulties, and CDSFL's claims may not be divisible that way. It also requires a population-wide census, which is a central-server operation.

mechanisms.name: Adaptive replication (pessimistic prior plus probation streak)
mechanisms.what_it_does: "Basic replication-based validation reduces effective computing capacity by a factor of at least two. BOINC provides a refinement called adaptive replication that moves this factor close to one." The server maintains, per (host, app version), a count N of consecutive jobs validated by replication; once N exceeds a threshold, replication happens only sometimes, with probability going to zero as N grows. In the earlier error-rate form, if E(H) exceeds a constant K all jobs to that host are replicated; below K, replication is random with probability falling to zero. "The initial estimate of E(H) is sufficiently high that a host must complete some number of jobs correctly before it is eligible for non-replication."
mechanisms.citation: Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 3.4; Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.6. Exact formulas as reconstructed by Christoforou, Fernández Anta, Georgiou, Mosteiro and Sánchez, "Coping with Unreliable Workers in Internet-based Computing: An Evaluation of Reputation Mechanisms", arXiv:1307.2783v4, Figure 1: Legacy BOINC beta(0) = 0.1, beta(r) = 0.95*beta(r-1) on a truthful round and beta(r-1) + 0.1 otherwise, reputation 0 while beta > 0.05 and 1 - sqrt(beta/0.05) otherwise; current BOINC reputation 0 while streak < 10 and 1 - 1/streak otherwise.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This is the single cleanest cold-start answer in the field, and it is not a tournament. Start every participant at an explicitly pessimistic prior (an assumed 10% error rate), require a probation streak (10 consecutive validated results) before any trust is granted, and let the replication probability decay smoothly thereafter. Cost of calibration is bounded and is spent on real work, not on a synthetic problem.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Reputation is held per (participant, task type) for the stated reason that reliability is not a single scalar. A participant trusted on one task class is untrusted on another until it has its own streak there.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers essentially unchanged and satisfies the founder's hard constraint that capability is measured. What breaks: it requires a validator that can decide whether two independently produced answers agree — which for CDSFL means a comparison function over proofs and falsifiers, not over floats. And the 10-sample probation per (seat, task type) is a real cost on a roster of 700: 7,000 replicated jobs before anyone is trusted.

mechanisms.name: Homogeneous redundancy and homogeneous app version, with per-class job-cache reservation
mechanisms.what_it_does: For numerically unstable applications, hosts are partitioned into equivalence classes by OS and CPU (coarse) or OS, CPU vendor and CPU model (fine), within which results are assumed bit-identical. Once an instance is dispatched, further replicas go only to the same class — the job is "committed to that HR class". Homogeneous app version does the same across app versions "for example, CPU and GPU versions may compute valid but incomparable results". Because the job cache then fills with committed jobs and other classes starve, a Census program builds a per-class table of recent average credit and N slots are reserved per class, N proportional to that class's recent average credit "and is at least 1", with a fraction of slots reserved for uncommitted jobs.
mechanisms.citation: Taufer, M., Anderson, D., Cicotti, P. and Brooks, C.L. III, "Homogeneous Redundancy: a Technique to Ensure Integrity of Molecular Simulation Results Using Public Computing", Heterogeneous Computing Workshop, IPDPS 2005; Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.4; Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 3.4
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start mechanism, but it constrains one: a participant in a rare equivalence class gets at least 1 reserved cache slot, so it is never starved to zero.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It is the admission that some participants' outputs are simply not comparable to others', and that the right response is partitioning plus a guaranteed capacity floor per partition, not a global ranking.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Highly relevant and under-appreciated. Comparing a frontier model's answer against a small model's answer is the "numerically unstable application" problem: the outputs may both be valid and still not agree. If CDSFL replicates a claim across heterogeneous seats and demands agreement, it has imported exactly this failure. The literature's fix is to confine the quorum to a comparability class and then reserve capacity per class so small classes do not starve. What breaks if adopted: cross-model comparison — the thing the founder most wants — becomes impossible inside a quorum, and must move to an explicit adjudication layer instead.

mechanisms.name: Host punishment via a daily quota that shrinks on error and doubles on success
mechanisms.what_it_does: A project sets a limit on job instances downloadable by a host per day, and "the limit scales with the number of processors available on the host". "if a host reports a job instance that experienced an error then that host's daily limit is reduced by one. Thus a host who experiences nothing but errors will be eventually limited to only one job instance per day. Once the problem has been corrected on the host, it will start to return successful job instances. As successful job instances are returned, then the limit is doubled until it reaches the limit set by the project." The CreditNew design adds host_app_version fields error_rate, scale_probation and max_jobs_per_day, and puts a host on scale probation with its error rate reset to an initial value when a result's peak FLOP count exceeds the workunit's fpops_bound.
mechanisms.citation: Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.10; BOINC wiki "CreditNew" (github.com/BOINC/boinc/wiki/CreditNew)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Indirectly: it bounds the damage a miscalibrated prior can do, since a participant that errors constantly converges to 1 job per day rather than consuming unbounded capacity.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The quota scales with declared processor count, so the floor is proportional, not absolute.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and satisfies the founder's hard constraint better than anything else in the field: the floor is 1 job per day, never 0, so no participant is ever permanently set aside, and recovery is automatic and geometric (doubling) so a participant that improves climbs back without human intervention. This is the mechanism the founder should adopt in place of promotion tiers. What breaks: nothing structural; it needs a per-seat daily counter and an error signal.

mechanisms.name: Score-based matchmaking S(J,H) as a reweightable linear combination
mechanisms.what_it_does: "This is done using a scoring function S(J, H). The job assignment policy is essentially to send H the cached jobs J for which S(J, H) is greatest. The default scoring function is a linear combination of" expected FLOPS of the fastest available app version; whether the volunteer selected the job's application; whether the job is already committed to the host's homogeneous-redundancy class; -(A-B)^2 for job-size/host-speed mismatch in standard-deviation units; the job's disk and RAM requirements; and whether a non-replicated job has been chosen for this host. "Projects can adjust the weights of these terms, or they can replace the scoring function entirely." The 2019 version adds keyword preferences, submitter allocation balance, whether the job was skipped on a previous request, and locality (whether the host already holds the input files).
mechanisms.citation: Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.8; Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 6.4
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Each term degrades gracefully: when the measured capability term is unavailable it falls back to the declared prior, and the other terms (class commitment, locality, submitter balance) are available immediately.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: By composing several independent criteria rather than collapsing capability to one number, and by letting operators reweight the composition per deployment.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the architecture CDSFL should copy rather than a tier ladder. It is additive in the founder's sense: each new measured property becomes one more weighted term with a named caller, and the whole thing is one function that can be tested. What breaks: weights are hand-set, and Anderson and Reed concede they were never validated in the field.

mechanisms.name: Reliable-host routing for retries and stragglers
mechanisms.what_it_does: "the BOINC identifies hosts that have a history of returning valid results quickly. Retries are then sent preferentially to these hosts. Since these hosts are also known to return work quickly, the deadline for the job instance is also reduced." In current configuration, hosts count as reliable on turnaround-time and error-rate criteria; jobs at or above reliable_on_priority are treated as need-reliable and routed preferentially to reliable hosts with the delay bound multiplied by reliable_reduced_delay_bound.
mechanisms.citation: Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.7; BOINC wiki "ProjectOptions" (reliable_on_priority, reliable_reduced_delay_bound, reliable_priority_on_over) [VERIFY:current — the default value of reliable_reduced_delay_bound was reported to me as approximately 0.5 and I did not read the page body directly]
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A new participant is simply not reliable yet, and receives only ordinary-priority work. No calibration round is needed; eligibility is earned on real jobs.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Reliability is a composite of correctness AND turnaround, measured, not declared.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly, and is the right place for the founder's "top tier" intuition. Rather than promoting seats to a tier that gets the hardest work, mark CERTAIN CLAIMS as needing a reliable seat (a blocking falsification, a settled-merge decision) and route only those preferentially, with a tightened deadline. Everything else goes to everyone. What breaks: it needs a per-claim priority field, which CDSFL's severity class could supply.

mechanisms.name: Threshold-based scheduling on measured availability and reliability, with a measured optimum and a named starvation failure
mechanisms.what_it_does: Defines availability_i(t) = WUIcompleted_i(t) / WUIdistributed_i(t) and reliability_i(t) = WUIvalidated_i(t) / WUIcompleted_i(t), and assigns work only to workers above both thresholds. Trace-driven simulation over 340 hours of real Predictor@Home traces found a sweet spot bounded by 0.50 and 0.75 for both thresholds: successful results rose on average 14% (peak 18%) and valid results 13% (peak 17%) versus first-come-first-serve. Thresholds at either end of the range (0 or 0.95) gave "unacceptable" performance — at 0 the master is flooded with unsuccessful and invalid results, at 0.95 too few workers qualify and "the search space of the BOINC application reduces". The paper states the failure mode explicitly: "This policy has the disadvantage of starving workers that are considered to be unsuitable to perform the work at hand and, thus, virtually removes these workers from a project. To alleviate this situation, a policy could allow workers to improve their ratings. But, this can only be achieved by assigning WUIs to these 'unsuitable' workers". Future work proposed dynamic thresholds plus "assigning low-priority replicas to workers with availability and reliability ratings below the thresholds". It also reports that "an available worker is not necessarily a reliable one" — the two metrics are not correlated.
mechanisms.citation: Estrada, T., Flores, D.A., Taufer, M., Teller, P.J., Kerstens, A. and Anderson, D.P., "The Effectiveness of Threshold-Based Scheduling Policies in BOINC Projects", 2nd IEEE International Conference on e-Science and Grid Computing (e-Science '06), p. 88 (PDF at cs.unm.edu/~estrada/trilce/uploads/Main/escience06_estrada.pdf)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does not, and says so. A worker with no history has undefined ratings, and the paper identifies the resulting exploration problem as unsolved in its own design.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It separates availability from correctness as two independent measured axes and shows empirically that they do not correlate, so a single capability scalar is wrong.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly, and it is the measured number the founder should want: the optimal promotion threshold is neither permissive nor strict but around 0.50 to 0.75, and both extremes are measurably worse than no filtering in at least one metric. The paper also hands CDSFL the fix for the founder's hard constraint: route LOW-PRIORITY replicas to below-threshold participants so they can earn their way back. What breaks: the 0.50 to 0.75 figure is from 2 molecular-biology applications on 1 project's traces, and the paper itself says the sweet spots differed slightly between the 2 applications and calls for wider study. Do not import the number; import the method.

mechanisms.name: Work Queue with Replication (knowledge-free scheduling)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Argues that schedulers for heterogeneous grids normally need information such as host speed, host load and task size, that this information is often unavailable or hard to obtain, and that a scheduler using NO such information performs well if it relies on task replication to absorb the heterogeneity and volatility. Replication delivers good and stable performance at the cost of extra resource consumption; bounding the replication factor keeps the overhead controlled with little performance loss.
mechanisms.citation: Paranhos da Silva, D., Cirne, W. and Brasileiro, F.V., "Trading Cycles for Information: Using Replication to Schedule Bag-of-Tasks Applications on Computational Grids", Euro-Par 2003, LNCS 2790, pp. 169-180
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It abolishes cold start by abolishing the capability model. Send the same task to k participants, take the first valid return, discard the rest. No prior, no ranking, no calibration round.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Implicitly and perfectly: the fastest capable participant wins each race, so the allocation is automatically correct without anyone ever estimating capability.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the direct competitor to the founder's second mechanism and it is strictly simpler. A knockout tournament spends capacity to learn a ranking and then uses the ranking to route; WQR spends the same capacity on redundancy and gets the right routing for free, continuously, with no ranking to go stale. For a roster whose membership and capability both change, that is the stronger design. What breaks if adopted: cost. The founder wants cost-effectiveness as a first-class objective, and WQR's whole premise is trading cycles for information. The bounded-replication result is what makes it affordable, and the bound is the parameter to measure.

mechanisms.name: HTCondor ClassAd matchmaking (symmetric advertisement, stateless matchmaker, match-as-hint)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Both sides of the market describe themselves in ONE symmetric language: "both servers and customers use the same language to describe their respective characteristics, constraints and preferences." Hard constraints go in a Requirements attribute, preferences in a Rank attribute. A policy-independent matchmaker discovers pairings and notifies the two parties, which then confirm the allocation through a separate bilateral claiming protocol; "a match is to be construed as a 'hint'", which is what keeps the matchmaker stateless. Gangmatching extends this to multilateral matches (job, machine, licence) by decomposing them into bilateral matches through nested "port" ClassAds.
mechanisms.citation: Raman, R., Livny, M. and Solomon, M., "Matchmaking: Distributed Resource Management for High Throughput Computing", 7th IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Distributed Computing (HPDC-7), Chicago, July 1998, pp. 140-147; Raman, R., "Matchmaking Frameworks for Distributed Resource Management", PhD dissertation (htcondor.com/doc/rajesh.dissert.pdf)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A participant with no history still advertises Requirements and Rank, so it is immediately matchable on declared attributes. There is no history requirement at all — which is also the weakness.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: By refusing to impose a fixed system model. The authors' explicit motivation is that "centralized resource managers with a fixed system model fit poorly in heterogeneous systems with decentralized ownership".
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The architecture transfers and is the best available answer to the founder's no-central-server requirement: a stateless matchmaker that issues non-binding hints, with the real commitment negotiated bilaterally, is close to what a peer-to-peer CDSFL would need. But Anderson and Reed name the disqualifying difference: "Condor assumes that worker nodes are trusted and have negligible error rate. There is no need for result validation, and there is no need for servers to maintain error rates or other information about worker nodes." They also state BOINC was designed for "scale two or three orders of magnitude larger than Condor". So ClassAds give CDSFL the matchmaking protocol and give it nothing at all on measured trust.

mechanisms.name: OurGrid Network of Favours (autonomous bilateral reciprocity, no central server)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each peer prioritises those who hold credit in its own past history of bilateral interactions, as an automated peer-to-peer reciprocation algorithm that ranks peers by their sharing. Reputation is stored locally by the peers who directly interacted with the participant, and "reputation never becomes negative, otherwise malicious users could just create a new identity with a clean reputation." Peers preferentially donate to those they owe the most favours to.
mechanisms.citation: Andrade, N., Brasileiro, F.V., Cirne, W. and Mowbray, M., "Discouraging Free Riding in a Peer-to-Peer CPU-Sharing Grid", HPDC-13, Honolulu, June 2004, pp. 129-137, DOI 10.1109/HPDC.2004.9; Cirne, W. et al., "OurGrid: An Approach to Easily Assemble Grids with Equitable Resource Sharing", JSSPP 2003 (Springer LNCS, DOI 10.1007/10968987_4). Deployed as the OurGrid Community since December 2004.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Deliberately badly, for a stated reason. A new peer starts at zero credit and receives only capacity nobody else wants. The design accepts this because a reputation floor of zero is what makes Sybil identities worthless — a fresh identity gains exactly nothing. Cold start cost is the price of resistance to re-identification.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Only through what each peer chooses to donate; there is no global capability model, by design.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as the answer to "no central server beyond the endpoints": purely local, pairwise, non-negative reputation requires no coordinator and no global state. What breaks, and it is fatal to the founder's framing: it produces NO global ranking. Each peer has its own private ordering over the peers it has transacted with, and there is no bracket, no tier and no roster-wide order. If CDSFL wants a global capability ranking it needs a coordinator to assemble it; if it wants no coordinator it must give up the global ranking. That is a genuine either-or, not an engineering detail.

mechanisms.name: BitTorrent choking with optimistic unchoking (the founder's own named analogy, with its cold-start slot)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each peer keeps a fixed number of upload slots (reference default 4) and ranks candidates by measured recent throughput, using a 20-second moving average with the choke/unchoke decision re-made every 10 seconds, long enough for TCP to reach full rate. One slot is reserved for a RANDOMLY chosen peer that has not earned it — the optimistic unchoke — rotated every 30 seconds. Optimistic unchokes serve two jobs: bootstrapping new peers that hold nothing yet into the reciprocation game without requiring reciprocation, and continuous resource discovery to find better partners than the current top four. Choking is a refusal to upload, not a disconnect, so the connection need not be renegotiated.
mechanisms.citation: Cohen, B., "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent", 1st Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (IPTPS/P2PEcon), 2003, bittorrent.org/bittorrentecon.pdf. Critique: Piatek, M., Isdal, T., Anderson, T., Krishnamurthy, A. and Venkataramani, A., "Do Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent?", NSDI 2007 (homes.cs.washington.edu/~arvind/papers/bittyrant.pdf). [VERIFY:current — sources disagree on the slot count: Cohen's description implies 1 optimistic slot among 4, while Piatek et al. report the reference client optimistically unchokes 2 peers every 30 seconds; this probably reflects client versions.]
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This is the mechanism, in the system the founder named. There is no calibration round. Capability is a continuously-maintained measured throughput average, and a fixed fraction of capacity (1 slot in 4, or 25%) is permanently reserved for randomly chosen unproven peers. Exploration is a standing budget line, not a startup phase.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Badly, and this is the measured failure. Piatek et al. found that "sufficiently low bandwidth peers almost never earn reciprocation, while high capacity peers send much faster than the minimal rate required for reciprocation". Pure throughput-ranked reciprocity starves the weak end of a heterogeneous population.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and should replace the founder's tournament. Permanently reserve a fixed fraction of dispatch for randomly selected seats regardless of measured standing, re-rank on a short trailing window, and never disconnect a seat — just stop sending it work this round. That satisfies all of "measured capability", "no permanent exclusion" and "works at any roster size" with one mechanism and no bracket. What breaks: Piatek's finding. If CDSFL ranks on raw throughput, the small-model end of the roster will be starved exactly as low-bandwidth BitTorrent peers are, and the founder's heterogeneity constraint will be violated by the very mechanism meant to honour it. The fix in this literature is the size-class mechanism above: rank within a size class, not across the whole population.

mechanisms.name: Sarmenta spot-checking, blacklisting, and credibility-based fault tolerance
mechanisms.what_it_does: Voting lowers the error rate exponentially in redundancy but requires all work to be done at least twice and degrades badly when many participants are bad. Spot-checking instead slips tasks with KNOWN answers into the ordinary workload and checks whether participants return them correctly; this lowers the error rate linearly in the amount of work while adding only a small fraction to running time. Paired with blacklisting (removing a participant that fails a spot-check) it is far cheaper than voting. The paper's main contribution is credibility-based fault tolerance, which attaches probability estimates to both results and workers and uses them to direct redundancy where it is needed; combining voting with spot-checking lets an already linearly-reduced error rate shrink exponentially, validated by Monte Carlo simulation.
mechanisms.citation: Sarmenta, L.F.G., "Sabotage-tolerance mechanisms for volunteer computing systems", Future Generation Computer Systems 18(4), pp. 561-572 (2001/2002), DOI via ScienceDirect S0167739X01000772; full analysis in Sarmenta's 2001 MIT PhD thesis "Volunteer Computing" (people.csail.mit.edu/lfgs/bayanihan/papers/sarmenta-phd-mit2001.pdf). Anderson and Reed note Bayanihan's spot-checking "is similar to BOINC's adaptive replication". Later adopted as the basis of iExec's Proof-of-Contribution protocol.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Spot-checking IS a cold-start probe, but a continuous one embedded in real work rather than a separate calibration round. There is no distinction between the calibration phase and the production phase.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Credibility is a per-participant probability that directs how much redundancy each result needs, so weak or unproven participants are not excluded, their results are simply weighted and replicated more.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the closest named match to the founder's "give everyone a hard problem with a known answer", and it transfers with one important correction: do NOT run it as a separate up-front round. Mix graded problems with known answers into the ordinary claim stream at a low rate, forever, so the capability estimate never goes stale and no capacity is spent on a dedicated tournament. What breaks: Sarmenta's blacklisting half violates the founder's no-permanent-exclusion constraint and should be replaced by the BOINC quota mechanism. And the collusion assumption fails — iExec's own design notes concede that "the main drawback of Sarmenta's article is the assumption that Byzantine workers are not working together", which matters for CDSFL because seats drawn from the same vendor or the same base model are correlated by construction.

mechanisms.name: Folding@home reference-machine credit plus quick-return bonus with a probation gate
mechanisms.what_it_does: Base credit is set by timing each project on a single reference machine, so points are relative to that one machine and a faster system earns proportionally more. The delivered points are final_points = base_points * max(1, sqrt(k * deadline_length / elapsed_time)), with k defaulting to 0.75 and varying by project so that more scientifically valuable projects can carry a higher k. The bonus requires a passkey, at least 10 successfully returned bonus-eligible work units, an overall return rate of at least 80% on assigned units, and return before the timeout; it is not awarded for partial returns. The project states that the benchmark machine "evens out a lot of this", that "variation between WUs and between donor machines is unavoidable", and that "the goal is fairness across projects, not exact agreement with any one machine". Separately, its dispatch is a two-level scheduler in which clients contact a master scheduler that directs them to one of several job queues.
mechanisms.citation: Folding@home Points FAQ (foldingathome.org/faq/points/) [VERIFY:current — the k default and the reference-machine specification are present-day configuration and the forum reports of an Intel Core i5 750 at 2.67 GHz as the benchmark machine are community sources, not the current FAQ]. Two-level scheduler described in Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 5, which notes "Details of its infrastructure have not been published". Original project: Larson, S.M., Snow, C.D., Shirts, M. and Pande, V.S., "Folding@Home and Genome@Home", Computational Genomics, Horizon Press, 2002.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: With an explicit probation gate that is strikingly close to BOINC's: 10 completed units and an 80% completion rate before the speed bonus applies at all. Before that, a participant earns base credit only — it is never excluded, just not yet bonused.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: By declaring ONE reference machine as the common denominator and expressing everyone's contribution relative to it, rather than attempting mutual comparison across the population. Fairness is defined across projects, not across machines, and the project says so.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The pattern transfers well and is cheap: pick one reference seat, time every task class on it once, express every other seat's work relative to that single denominator, and gate any speed-based reward behind a minimum of 10 completions and an 80% completion rate. This gets a comparable cross-seat number without any tournament and without any pairwise comparison. What breaks: the reference machine is a single point of definitional failure — when it is retired, every historical number silently changes meaning — and the project concedes the choice "has implications for points for donors".

mechanisms.name: BOINC credit: three successive systems, all of which failed, and the developer's own verdict
mechanisms.what_it_does: Three generations of attempts to compute one comparable number per participant. System 1 was peak-FLOPS-based, C = H.whetstone * J.cpu_time; "The problem with this system is that, for a given app version, efficiency can vary widely between hosts", which made credit for identical jobs "arbitrary and unfair". System 2 was actual-FLOPs-based; "It doesn't address GPUs properly; projects using GPUs have to write custom code" and "It doesn't prevent credit cheating when single replication is used". System 3, CreditNew, defines PFC(J) = sum over resources of runtime * usage * peak_flops, then applies version normalisation (ratio to the most efficient version's average) and host normalisation (ratio of the (host, app version) average to the app-version average), with host_scale capped at a constant "say, 10" and one credit unit defined as one day of a 1 GFLOPS Whetstone CPU (cobblestone_scale = 200/86400e9). Its own page concedes PFC(J) "is not reliable; cheaters can falsify elapsed time or device attributes" and that "The host punishment mechanism doesn't deal effectively with cherry picking". Efficiency is "very roughly, 10% for GPUs, 50% for CPUs", and GPUs have 10 to 100 times the peak FLOPS of CPUs. The designer's own retrospective: CreditNew "is complicated and I'm not sure it ever worked exactly as I intended" and was "wildly unpopular".
mechanisms.citation: BOINC wiki "CreditNew" (github.com/BOINC/boinc/wiki/CreditNew); Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 7 — "The efficiency of a CPU application can vary by a factor of 2 between computers; hence computing credit based on runtime and benchmarks would violate device neutrality. The problem is worse for GPUs"; designer's retrospective quoted at continuum-hypothesis.com/boinc_history.php; independent critique at wiki.atlas.aei.uni-hannover.de/EinsteinAtHome/BOINC/EvaluationOfCreditNew [VERIFY:current — whether CreditNew is still the default was not confirmed for 2026]
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Badly, and it is documented: the Einstein@Home evaluation reports "GPU efficiency defaults that guarantee underestimate before host scales become active" and that initial time estimates for a new GPU app can be off by a large factor.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It is the 20-year record of failing to. Three attempts, each defeated by the fact that efficiency (actual divided by peak) varies by a factor of 2 across CPUs and far more across GPUs.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Do not copy this; read it as the field's negative result. Three stated goals — device neutrality, project neutrality, cheat resistance — were pursued for two decades across three rewrites and never jointly achieved. The transferable lesson for CDSFL is a prohibition: do not build a single scalar capability-or-contribution score that must simultaneously be comparable across heterogeneous seats, comparable across task types, and resistant to a seat misreporting its own effort. Use several task-type-specific measured quantities, each with a named consumer, instead.

mechanisms.name: Benchmark-based capability estimation (Whetstone and Dhrystone) and the efficiency problem
mechanisms.what_it_does: The client periodically runs the Whetstone benchmark for floating-point speed and Dhrystone for integer speed, launching one copy per CPU simultaneously for 15 seconds each so that multicore contention is reflected. Peak FLOPS for a CPU is the Whetstone score; for a GPU it comes from a manufacturer-supplied formula using the higher of single or double precision. The documented limitation: "Other factors such as memory-system speed affect application performance, so a job may take the same CPU time on a 1 GFLOPS host as on a 10 GFLOPS host." The ratio of actual to peak is called efficiency. SETI@home separately banned client modifications because volunteers were recompiling the client for their own processors and the project "didn't want SETI@home to be used in benchmark wars", and because "We didn't trust the correctness of such modifications".
mechanisms.citation: BOINC documentation on client benchmarks and CreditNew (boinc.berkeley.edu/trac/wiki/CreditNew); Anderson, D.P., Cobb, J., Korpela, E., Lebofsky, M. and Werthimer, D., "SETI@home: an experiment in public-resource computing", Communications of the ACM 45(11), pp. 56-61, November 2002, DOI 10.1145/581571.581573; see also the BOINC "AutoFlops" wiki page, now marked "DEPRECATED: HISTORICAL INTEREST ONLY"
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the cheapest possible cold-start prior and it is what BOINC falls back to when no history exists. It costs 15 seconds, not a hard mathematics problem.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It does not. Efficiency on the actual application is what matters, and benchmark score does not predict it — a factor of 2 spread on CPUs, worse on GPUs.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the direct verdict on the founder's cold-start mechanism, and it is unfavourable. A synthetic calibration problem is a benchmark. This field ran benchmarks on hundreds of thousands of participants for 20 years and concluded that a benchmark score is "acceptable as an approximate measure" for a PRIOR and nothing more, because performance on the real workload is what determines allocation and the benchmark does not predict it. The abandoned AutoFlops design even proposed "a fixed 'reference job' run on all machines" and was deprecated. The SETI@home finding adds a second warning: once participants know a benchmark determines their standing, they optimise for the benchmark, and the project's response was to ban the optimisation outright.

mechanisms.name: Resource prioritization versus exclusion versus replication, measured against optimal
mechanisms.what_it_does: Compares three selection techniques on trace-driven simulations of four desktop-grid configurations. Prioritizing by clock rate (PRI-CR) beats first-come-first-serve but still lands more than a factor of 4 from optimal for 100 five-minute tasks. PRI-HISTORY, which predicts each host's expected operations per availability interval from the previous weekday's trace, "achieves poor performance" — the measured average prediction error using the previous day as a predictor was 110 minutes in operations and 108 minutes in time, against tasks mostly under 2 hours, because availability-interval size "was not stationary across weekdays". Excluding hosts 0.5 to 1 standard deviation below the mean clock rate (mean 1.2 GHz, standard deviation 730 MHz on the SDSC platform) brings substantial benefit; excluding at 0.25 standard deviations "excludes so many hosts that it not only removes the 'slow' hosts but also excludes the useful ones"; excluding at 1.5 standard deviations excludes too few. The best combination of prioritization, exclusion and replication reaches within a factor of 1.7 of optimal.
mechanisms.citation: Kondo, D., Chien, A.A. and Casanova, H., "Resource Management for Rapid Application Turnaround on Enterprise Desktop Grids", SC '04 (ACM/IEEE Supercomputing), Pittsburgh, 2004, p. 17 (PDF at henricasanova.github.io/files/papers/kondo_sc04.pdf); journal version "Scheduling Task Parallel Applications for Rapid Turnaround on Enterprise Desktop Grids", Journal of Grid Computing 5, pp. 379-405 (2007), DOI 10.1007/s10723-007-9063-y, whose abstract states that "ranking desktop resources according to their clock rates, without taking into account their availability history, is surprisingly effective"
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It argues cold start barely matters: a static declared attribute, available instantly and free, outperformed a measured history model.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: With a measured optimum for exclusion aggressiveness, roughly 0.5 to 1 standard deviation below the population mean, with both more and less aggressive settings measurably worse.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers as a falsifier rather than a design. Its finding is the strongest published argument against the founder's whole premise, and the reason is stated precisely: measured capability only pays when the measurement is STATIONARY over a horizon longer than the task. Kondo's hosts had a 110-minute day-to-day prediction error against sub-2-hour tasks, so measurement lost to a static attribute. Before CDSFL spends a calibration round, it must measure its own seats' day-to-day capability autocorrelation against the duration of a claim. If capability drifts faster than claims complete, the ranking is noise and a cheap declared prior plus replication wins.

mechanisms.name: Successive Halving and Hyperband (the founder's recursive difficulty ladder, already named)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Successive Halving spreads a fixed budget evenly across all surviving candidates, scores them, discards the weaker half, and repeats on the survivors with roughly double the per-candidate budget, until one remains. Its working assumption is that rankings at low fidelity predict rankings at high fidelity. Its two parameters — total budget and number of candidates — must be fixed in advance and are hard to set, so Hyperband runs several Successive Halving brackets with different breadth-versus-depth tradeoffs and hedges across them. Jamieson and Talwalkar's contribution is that the method works in the NON-stochastic case, where losses are not independent identically distributed draws and the usual statistical bounds do not apply, because the algorithm does not adapt mid-round.
mechanisms.citation: Karnin, Z., Koren, T. and Somekh, O., "Almost Optimal Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits", ICML 2013 (original Successive Halving); Jamieson, K. and Talwalkar, A., "Non-stochastic Best Arm Identification and Hyperparameter Optimization", AISTATS 2016, PMLR 51:240-248 (proceedings.mlr.press/v51/jamieson16.pdf); Li, L., Jamieson, K., DeSalvo, G., Rostamizadeh, A. and Talwalkar, A., "Hyperband: A Novel Bandit-Based Approach to Hyperparameter Optimization", arXiv:1603.06560, JMLR 18(185), 2018
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It IS a cold-start algorithm with a proven budget guarantee: no prior is needed, every candidate starts equal, and the elimination schedule is what bounds the total cost.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Only along the one axis being scored. It produces a single total order, which is its limitation here.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The founder's first mechanism — give everyone a hard problem, promote the top, give the rest an easier problem, recurse — is Successive Halving with difficulty as the budget axis, and his second mechanism is a knockout bracket, which is noisy tournament ranking. Both are named, analysed and bounded in this literature, so the honest answer to "am I reinventing the wheel" is yes, with a known name and known guarantees. What breaks if adopted as stated: Successive Halving DISCARDS the losing half, which violates the founder's hard constraint that no participant is ever permanently set aside; and it yields a single scalar order, which the volunteer-computing evidence says is the wrong shape for capability. Hyperband's bracket hedging is the honest fix for the first problem, but the second is structural.

mechanisms.name: Peer-to-peer data distribution in a volunteer-computing system, and why it is not used
mechanisms.what_it_does: A modified BOINC client distributes executables and input files over a peer-to-peer system rather than from project servers, to reduce server load and outgoing bandwidth. Anderson's own assessment: "This method hasn't been used by any projects, but it may be useful in the future." The field also states the architectural baseline plainly: "Volunteer computing uses central servers. There is typically no peer-to-peer communication", and SETI@home's own paper records that "There is no communication between clients."
mechanisms.citation: Elwaer, A., Harrison, A., Kelley, I. and Taylor, I., "Attic: A Case Study for Distributing Data in BOINC Projects", IEEE 9th International Symposium on Parallel and Distributed Processing with Applications Workshops, Busan, 2011; Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 9 and reference [45]; BOINC wiki "VolunteerComputing"; Anderson et al., CACM 45(11), 2002
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not applicable — it addresses data distribution, not work allocation.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Only in bandwidth terms.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The transferable finding is a boundary, and it is the one the founder most needs to hear. The largest and longest-running systems in this field are star-topology by construction, and the one serious peer-to-peer extension to the leading platform was built, published and then used by zero projects. The reason is structural: validation needs either a quorum (which requires someone to assemble and compare the replicas) or a spot-check answer key (which requires someone to hold the keys). OurGrid shows the only known escape — purely bilateral local reputation — and the price is that no global ranking exists. A peer-to-peer CDSFL is possible; a peer-to-peer CDSFL that also produces a roster-wide capability ranking has no precedent in this literature.

is_the_wheel_already_invented: Yes, substantially, and under names the founder can cite. His cold-start mechanism — a graded calibration task whose result is persisted and consumed by the router — is BOINC "probe jobs" (Anderson and Reed, HICSS, section 4.9) in its once-per-host form, and Sarmenta spot-checking (FGCS 18(4):561-572) in its continuous form. Its recursive-difficulty structure is Successive Halving (Karnin et al., ICML 2013; Jamieson and Talwalkar, AISTATS 2016). His knockout-tournament mechanism is noisy tournament ranking, and its closest competitor in this specific field is Work Queue with Replication (Paranhos, Cirne and Brasileiro, Euro-Par 2003), which argues you should skip the ranking entirely and spend the same capacity on replication. His "don't pitch a desktop PC against a supercomputer" constraint is BOINC job-size matching with size classes and quantiles (HICSS section 4.5; BOINC JobSizeMatching wiki; Anderson arXiv:1903.01699 section 3.5). His "capability is measured, never a name" constraint is proj_flops(H,V), a per-(participant, task-type) sample mean with a three-tier fallback and a sample threshold of 10 (arXiv:1903.01699 section 6.3). His "no participant is ever permanently set aside" constraint is BOINC host punishment, where the daily quota floor is 1 job rather than 0 and recovery is by doubling (HICSS section 4.10) — and Estrada et al. (e-Science '06) measured and named the starvation failure that occurs without it. His BitTorrent analogy already contains the answer: optimistic unchoking permanently reserves one upload slot in four for a randomly chosen unproven peer (Cohen, IPTPS 2003). Three things are NOT already invented. A roster-wide capability ranking with no coordinator: OurGrid's bilateral Network of Favours (HPDC 2004) is the only serverless reciprocity scheme here and it deliberately produces no global order. A device-neutral, task-neutral, cheat-resistant single capability number: three BOINC credit systems over 20 years and the designer's own verdict that CreditNew "is complicated and I'm not sure it ever worked exactly as I intended". And a field validation of any of it: Anderson and Reed wrote of their own matchmaking scheme, "we currently are unable to quantify how well they work."
strongest_disagreement:
The literature contradicts the founder on four specific points, and the first is the sharpest.

FIRST, AND MOST SERIOUS: measured capability history can be WORSE than a cheap static attribute. Kondo, Chien and Casanova (SC '04, p. 17; journal version Journal of Grid Computing 5:379-405, 2007) built exactly the founder's mechanism — PRI-HISTORY, which predicts each host's future throughput from measured past performance — and it "achieves poor performance". The reason is measured, not asserted: availability-interval size "was not stationary across weekdays", with an average prediction error of 110 minutes in operations and 108 minutes in time against tasks mostly under 2 hours. Their journal abstract states that "ranking desktop resources according to their clock rates, without taking into account their availability history, is surprisingly effective". A cheap static declared attribute beat the measurement. This does not refute the founder's constraint that capability must be measured rather than assumed from a name, but it does refute the assumption that an up-front measurement round pays for itself. It names the precondition: measurement pays only when capability is stationary over a horizon longer than one task. CDSFL has not measured its own seats' day-to-day capability autocorrelation against claim duration, and until it has, the calibration round is unjustified. Estrada et al. (e-Science '06) explicitly record their disagreement with Kondo on this and attribute it to different traces and task lengths — so this is a live, unresolved dispute in the published record, not a settled result either way.

SECOND: giving every participant the hardest problem first is the wrong direction. BOINC's job-size mechanism sends LARGER jobs to FASTER participants, but it determines who is faster from observed runtimes on ordinary work, never by first issuing everyone the hardest item. The founder's ladder starts at maximum difficulty, so every participant that fails the first rung has produced zero usable output, and Kondo's clock-rate distributions are left-heavy — most of the population is at the slow end, so most of the calibration budget is burned. SETI@home's response to the same heterogeneity was to change the GLOBAL work-unit size, "revising the client to do more computation per work unit", while "never turn[ing] away a client asking for work" (CACM 45(11):56-61). The field's method is to size the work to the participant, not to grade the participant with the hardest work.

THIRD: a knockout bracket produces a single total order, and this literature says capability is not a scalar. BOINC maintains reputation and runtime statistics per (host, app version) and not per host, for the stated reason that "some computers are reliable for CPU jobs but unreliable for GPU jobs" (arXiv:1903.01699 section 3.4). Estrada et al. measured that "an available worker is not necessarily a reliable one" and that availability and reliability "are not directly correlated". CPU application efficiency varies by a factor of 2 between machines and GPU efficiency varies far more, roughly 10% versus 50% of peak (CreditNew). A bracket cannot represent a capability vector indexed by task type, and whichever task the bracket happens to use becomes the only dimension measured.

FOURTH: the no-central-server requirement conflicts with the ranking requirement. The BOINC project states that "Volunteer computing uses central servers. There is typically no peer-to-peer communication", and SETI@home's paper records that "There is no communication between clients." The one peer-to-peer extension to BOINC that was built and published (Elwaer et al., IPDPSW 2011) "hasn't been used by any projects". The only serverless reciprocity design in this field, OurGrid's Network of Favours (Andrade, Brasileiro, Cirne and Mowbray, HPDC-13, pp. 129-137), keeps reputation strictly local to each pairwise relationship and never lets it go negative, and consequently produces no global ranking at all. Validation requires either a quorum, which needs a party to assemble and compare replicas, or a spot-check answer key, which needs a party to hold the keys. The founder may have a peer-to-peer CDSFL or a roster-wide measured capability ranking. There is no published precedent for both.

And a fifth, as a warning rather than a disagreement: BitTorrent's own throughput-ranked reciprocity has a measured heterogeneity failure. Piatek et al. (NSDI 2007) found that "sufficiently low bandwidth peers almost never earn reciprocation". If CDSFL ranks seats on measured throughput across the whole roster, the small-model end will be starved by the very mechanism intended to honour the founder's heterogeneity constraint.
open_problems: No field validation of matchmaking. Anderson and Reed, having described the full BOINC job-selection machinery, wrote: "These mechanism are operational on World Community Grid and other BOINC projects, and they seem to work. However, we currently are unable to quantify how well they work. It is difficult to do controlled experiments in the context of a large volunteer computing project, because there are many factors that cannot be controlled, and because poorly-performing mechanism can waste lots of resources and perhaps drive away volunteers." The field's answer was emulation, not field measurement: EmBOINC for server policies (Estrada, Taufer and Anderson, Journal of Grid Computing 7, 2007) and a client emulator (Anderson, "Emulating Volunteer Computing Scheduling Policies", PCGrid 2011). CDSFL inherits this: if the founder builds the mechanism, he must plan the emulator alongside it, because the live system cannot be A/B tested.

Cold start for job-size matching is undocumented. The BOINC JobSizeMatching wiki page defines effective speed as hav.et.avg * host.available_frac and gives no fallback whatsoever for a participant with no samples. The gap is real, not an omission in my reading.

When a measured capability estimate has gone stale. Kondo's 110-minute day-to-day prediction error is the only published quantification I found of capability non-stationarity in this setting, and nobody has published a rule for detecting staleness or re-measuring on a schedule tied to the drift rate.

Whether reputation history helps at all. Kondo, Chien and Casanova (SC '04) found history-based prioritization poor; Estrada et al. (e-Science '06) found threshold policies on measured availability and reliability worth 13% to 14% more valid results, and explicitly attribute the disagreement to different traces and task lengths. The dispute is unresolved in the published record.

A device-neutral, project-neutral, cheat-resistant single capability or contribution score. Three BOINC credit systems over roughly 20 years, each defeated by efficiency variation, and the designer's own retrospective verdict that it "is complicated and I'm not sure it ever worked exactly as I intended". The CreditNew page itself concedes PFC(J) "is not reliable; cheaters can falsify elapsed time or device attributes" and that "The host punishment mechanism doesn't deal effectively with cherry picking".

Collusion among correlated participants. Sarmenta's credibility mechanisms assume saboteurs do not coordinate; iExec's own design notes concede "this assumption does not hold in our context" and fall back to random worker selection as a statistical mitigation. For CDSFL this is acute, because seats sharing a vendor, a base model or a subscription are correlated by construction, not by conspiracy.

Low-latency and dependent work. Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 10: "BOINC doesn't currently support low-latency computing, by which we mean the ability to complete a job or DAG of jobs as fast as possible, and to give an estimate of completion time in advance. Doing so would require a reworking of all the scheduling mechanisms. For example, job runtime estimation would need to use sample variance as well as sample mean, in order to bound the probability of deadline miss." CDSFL's falsification rounds are closer to a DAG with a latency target than to a bag of independent tasks, so this is the exact gap it sits in.

The straggler or tail problem. Listed as future work in the same section: "BOINC could add a mechanism to deal with the straggler effect: the tendency for a few jobs to delay the completion of the batch as a whole. The idea is assign these jobs to fast, reliable, and available computers, and possibly to replicate the jobs." See also Chernov, Nikitina and Ivashko, "Task Scheduling in Desktop Grids: Open Problems", Open Engineering 7(1):343-351, 2017, DOI 10.1515/eng-2017-0038, which lists "optimizing the final stage of batch computation" among its named open problems alongside optimal task grouping, the needle-in-a-haystack paradigm, and game-theoretical scheduling.

Fully decentralized capability ranking. I found no survey comparing distributed-hash-table against unstructured-overlay schedulers for this purpose, and PPVC's unstructured overlay reportedly needed message flooding with significant bandwidth cost. Ivashko, Chernov and Nikitina's survey (IEEE TPDS 29:2882-2895, 2018, DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2018.2850004) covers hierarchical and peer-to-peer desktop grids and ends by formulating open problems; I could not read its full text and recommend the founder obtain it, since it is the most directly relevant survey to his question. [VERIFY:current]

Availability modelling beyond the mean. Anderson, section 10: "When using host availability as part of job runtime estimation, BOINC uses the average availability. This doesn't take into account the possibility that unavailability occurs on large chunks, or that it occurs with a daily or weekly periodicity." Rate limits and quota windows on model endpoints are exactly chunked, periodic unavailability, so CDSFL will hit this immediately.

Whether a probe-measured capability predicts work-measured capability at all. This is the gap the founder's mechanism depends on and which nobody in this field has published a measurement of. BOINC had probe jobs available and still routed by live runtime statistics; the AutoFlops design proposed "a fixed 'reference job' run on all machines" and is now marked "DEPRECATED: HISTORICAL INTEREST ONLY". The correlation between calibration-task performance and production performance is, as far as I could establish, unmeasured — which makes it the single most valuable experiment CDSFL could run before building the ladder.
